summary.text: Plasma is a state of matter formed when another state, often a gas, is ionized to an appreciable degree, so it holds many charged particles.
Its charged particles make it electrically conductive and very sensitive to electromagnetic fields.
Though rarely encountered on Earth, an estimated 99.9% of all ordinary matter in the universe is plasma, and stars are almost pure balls of it.

items.prompt: Some particles in a lit neon sign's gas are charged while others stay neutral. What is such a state called?

options.label: A fully neutral gas
A partially ionized plasma
A solid crystal of ions
A liquid held together by electrons

items.explain: Depending on conditions, neutral particles may also be present, in which case plasma is called partially ionized, as in neon signs and lightning.

items.prompt: How could a lab turn a neutral gas into plasma?

options.label: Heat it, or subject it to a strong electromagnetic field
Cool it down until its atoms stop moving
Squeeze it until it turns liquid
Strip out every charged particle it has

items.explain: Plasma can be artificially generated, for example by heating a neutral gas or subjecting it to a strong electromagnetic field.

items.prompt: Why can't scientists say at exactly what point a heated gas becomes plasma?

options.label: It happens at one fixed temperature that is hard to measure
A heated gas never becomes plasma on Earth
The transition is not well defined and depends on context
Gas and plasma are simply the same thing

items.explain: Unlike the other phase transitions, the transition to plasma is a matter of interpretation, and whether a given degree of ionization suffices depends on the phenomenon being considered.

items.prompt: What about plasma makes it electrically conductive?

options.label: It is made of tightly bound neutral atoms
It is denser than any solid
It is always completely at rest
It contains a significant portion of charged particles

items.explain: Plasma consists of a significant portion of charged particles, and their presence makes it electrically conductive.

items.prompt: A friend says the fourth state of matter must be exotic and rare everywhere. How would you correct that?

options.label: Correct, since stars are made of other states and contain none of it
Rare on Earth, but nearly all ordinary matter in the universe is in that state
Correct, since it can only be made inside special laboratories
Wrong, since it is just as common in every room on Earth

items.explain: Plasma is the fourth state of matter and, while rarely encountered on Earth, an estimated 99.9% of ordinary matter in the universe is plasma.

items.prompt: In the 1920s, Irving Langmuir watched electrons carried from heated filaments through an ionized gas. What did it remind him of when naming it?

options.label: A river carrying sand downstream
Wind carrying sparks through the air
Blood carrying red and white corpuscles
A magnet pulling iron filings along

items.explain: Langmuir first used the term by analogy with blood plasma, since the transport of electrons reminded him of the way blood plasma carries corpuscles and germs.

beats.hook: Rare on Earth, it makes up nearly all of the ordinary matter in the universe.

paragraphs.heading: The fourth state
paragraphs.text: After solid, liquid and gas, plasma is often named the fourth state of matter. It forms when one of the other states, often a gas, has been ionized to a large degree, so that a big share of it is made of charged particles, ions and electrons. It becomes such a good conductor of electricity that long-range electric and magnetic fields control how it behaves.

paragraphs.heading: Rare here, common out there
paragraphs.text: Plasma is rarely encountered on Earth, yet an estimated 99.9% of ordinary matter in the universe is plasma. Stars are almost pure balls of it, and it dominates the thin gas between galaxies and inside galaxy clusters. Neon signs and lightning are examples closer to home. They are partially ionized plasmas, which means some neutral particles are still mixed in.

paragraphs.heading: How the charges act together
paragraphs.text: Its charged particles make plasma a conductor of electricity. Overall it is usually close to neutral: positive and negative charges in any sizeable region roughly balance, a property called quasineutrality. The particles are unbound, but they are not free of forces. Every moving charge creates currents and fields that act on the other charges and are acted on by them, so the plasma moves in collective ways and reacts strongly to fields applied from outside.

paragraphs.heading: Making and using plasma
paragraphs.text: People can make plasma, for example by heating a neutral gas or by putting it in a strong electromagnetic field. The way plasma responds to such fields is put to work in many technologies, including plasma televisions, plasma etching and efforts to develop fusion energy.

paragraphs.heading: No sharp boundary
paragraphs.text: Unlike the changes between solid, liquid and gas, the change into plasma has no clear-cut point. Whether a substance counts as plasma is a matter of interpretation and context. How much ionization is enough depends on which phenomenon is being studied.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name came from
paragraphs.text: Plasma science grew out of the history of electricity. Vasily Petrov and Humphry Davy each discovered the electric arc in 1803, and in 1831 Michael Faraday studied glowing electric discharges in thin gases. In 1879 William Crookes, who worked on low-pressure discharges, put forward the idea of a fourth state of matter. Irving Langmuir first used the word plasma in the 1920s. The way electrons were carried along reminded him of how blood plasma carries red and white blood cells and germs.

paragraphs.heading: Unusual plasmas
paragraphs.text: Some plasmas break the usual pattern. A non-neutral plasma has a large excess of one kind of charge, or is made of a single kind of particle, and electric fields dominate it; charged particle beams are one example. A dusty plasma holds tiny charged grains of dust, typically found in space, which pick up high charges and interact with each other. In the laboratory these are also called complex plasmas.
